name: Baking soda brushing

lead: Baking soda brushing means cleaning teeth with sodium bicarbonate, in a toothpaste that contains it or as a home paste. People use it to lift surface stain from coffee, tea and tobacco for cleaner, lighter teeth.

Sodium bicarbonate is a mild abrasive that scrubs extrinsic stain and plaque, and it buffers acid. A review summarised on Wikipedia describes it as a low-abrasive, effective stain remover with no adverse effects in clinical studies, though that rests on a single review. Clinical trials of commercial baking soda toothpastes mostly measured plaque removal.

paras: Users brush with a commercial baking soda paste or mix a little with water, usually a few times a week. It does not bleach the tooth, and most evidence concerns commercial formulations rather than home pastes.

Baking soda is low in abrasiveness compared with many abrasives, and clinical reports of harm are limited. Home pastes vary in texture and how often they are used, which changes how abrasive they are.

angle.text: Users brush with baking soda, in commercial toothpastes or as a home paste, to scrub surface stain for cleaner, lighter teeth. Sodium bicarbonate is an established toothpaste ingredient described as mildly abrasive.

lead: Baking soda brushing is the practice of cleaning teeth with sodium bicarbonate, either through commercial toothpastes that contain it or as a home-made paste, usually to lift surface stain and leave teeth looking brighter. A brighter, cleaner-looking smile is a staple of grooming advice, and baking soda is a low-cost, widely available way people pursue it. Sodium bicarbonate is also an ingredient in some mouthwashes, where it is described as having anticaries and abrasive properties [1].

A 2017 review reported on the Wikipedia tooth-whitening page describes baking soda as a low-abrasive, effective stain remover whose buffering properties may help against Streptococcus mutans, with no adverse effects reported in clinical studies; the page notes this rests on a single review [2].

Controlled human studies mainly concern commercial baking soda dentifrices and plaque removal. A 2008 report of five clinical studies compared baking soda toothpastes with non-baking-soda formulations on plaque removal [3].
infobox: 1801, Valentin Rose the Younger; first US factory 1846 [1]

paras: Sodium bicarbonate is a white, crystalline salt, usually sold as a fine powder. Its solutions are mildly alkaline, it reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide, and it gradually decomposes when heated above roughly 80 C. The pharmacist Valentin Rose the Younger is credited with discovering it in 1801, and in 1846 the bakers John Dwight and Austin Church opened the first US factory to make baking soda; Arm and Hammer, a leading US brand, began a 1972 campaign promoting it as an odour absorber [1].

In oral care it appears in commercial toothpastes and mouthwashes, and some people mix it with water to make a paste for brushing. A paste of baking soda and a little water is described as a gentle scouring powder, which is the property used on teeth [1].

In looksmaxxing and tooth-care circles baking soda is one of several low-cost do-it-yourself approaches to removing stain. It is often combined with other household ingredients, which are covered in separate entries. T Nation posters have described rinsing with and then brushing with baking soda before a minty mouthwash, and one poster describes adding hydrogen peroxide to the routine on a dentist's recommendation [4][5].

Wikipedia distinguishes extrinsic stains, which sit on the tooth surface and come from smoking, tea, coffee, red wine and some mouthwashes, from intrinsic stains formed inside the tooth, which are the main target of bleaching because cleaning cannot remove them [2]. Abrasive whitening toothpastes contain more abrasives and detergents than regular pastes, and some add low peroxide concentrations that lighten shade by about one or two shades with continued use [2].

The page calls baking soda a safe, low-abrasive option for stain removal and whitening, presenting it as gentler than excessively abrasive whitening toothpastes, and notes its acid-buffering properties and antibacterial action at high concentrations [2]. Evidence for it as a whitening agent beyond surface stain is limited, and it is not a bleaching agent.

Plaque removal has been better studied: an earlier clinical study showed that brushing with a baking soda dentifrice removed significantly more plaque than two commercial pastes without it, and the 2008 five-study report compared baking soda dentifrices with more recent non-baking-soda formulations [3].

Wikipedia reports that whitening is the most promoted method in cosmetic dentistry, citing over 100 million Americans using some form of whitening and about $15 billion spent in 2010. Methods range from store-bought strips and gels to in-office treatments [2]. Baking soda is the home option within that market, alongside oil pulling and other household remedies that Wikipedia traces to ancient and medieval practice [2].

The review summary says clinical studies reported no adverse effects of baking soda toothpaste, though it rests on one source [2]. General dental guidance, as summarised on Wikipedia, notes that brushing too hard causes abrasion regardless of the paste [6]. The main listed hazard of sodium bicarbonate itself is eye irritation [1].

Wikipedia's account of whitening history notes that some old remedies, such as a late-seventeenth-century barber practice of filing and applying acid, caused lasting enamel damage, and that carbamide peroxide can roughen enamel; excessive abrasion is the general concern with scrubbing agents [2].

A 2008 report in the Journal of Clinical Dentistry described five clinical studies comparing commercial baking soda dentifrices with non-baking-soda toothpastes for plaque removal [3]. No clinical trials of home-made baking soda pastes for whitening were identified.

lore.intro: Baking soda comes up on forums as a cheap alternative to whitening strips and as a household remedy used with other products [4][5].

claims.claim: Baking soda works better than whitening strips.
Baking soda with hydrogen peroxide whitens teeth.
Baking soda is gentle enough to use daily.
